**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve lower VB slots when rebinding non-zero firstBinding**

This replay path rebuilds a fresh zero-initialized `vb` array per command and then calls `set_vertex_buffers(pipe, first + count, vb)`, which redefines slots `[0, first)` as NULL whenever `firstBinding > 0`. In command buffers that bind slot 0 first and later bind slot 1+ (a valid Vulkan pattern), the later bind unintentionally drops earlier bindings before draw, causing missing/incorrect vertex fetch. Gallium's `set_vertex_buffers` API is consecutive-from-zero state, so this path needs persisted vertex-buffer state (or merge with previous bindings) rather than zeroing unspecified lower slots.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Return a valid Vulkan error code for create-time limits**

The new oversize-attachment guard returns `VK_ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED`, but `vkCreateFramebuffer` does not list that as an allowed return code. This can surface as API-conformance failures (especially with validation layers off) when apps hit this path, because callers are only required to handle the function’s specified error set. The same return-code pattern was added in `r300vk_CreateRenderPass` as well and should be aligned to an allowed `VkResult`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Use allowed VkResult in CreateRenderPass limit checks**

These new limit guards return `VK_ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED`, but `vkCreateRenderPass` only advertises `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY`, `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_HOST_MEMORY`, `VK_ERROR_UNKNOWN`, and `VK_ERROR_VALIDATION_FAILED` as failure codes. Returning an unspecified code here can break strict callers and conformance expectations when the guard triggers, so the failure path should use one of the command’s valid `VkResult` values.

nodes.body: In the NIR direct path, r300_nir_lower_for_rc() mutates the NIR in-place (including ntr_fixup_varying_slots). This VS code can be compiled multiple times for different derived states (e.g., wpos variants in r300_pick_vertex_shader), so lowering the same vs->state.ir.nir repeatedly will corrupt locations/semantics. Clone the NIR before lowering/RC emission (as done in r300_fs.c) and free the clone after compilation, keeping vs->state.ir.nir unmodified for subsequent compiles.

r300vk_MapMemory: when offset < mem->memory_offset, the code clamps resource_offset to 0. This can map the wrong region silently and can also hide underflow/out-of-bounds cases (e.g., offset+size not within the bound resource). Instead, validate that offset >= memory_offset and that the requested range fits within the underlying PIPE_BUFFER size, returning VK_ERROR_MEMORY_MAP_FAILED on invalid ranges.

r300vk_MapMemory: the texture path ignores the Vulkan offset/size parameters and always maps mip 0 full surface. This makes vkMapMemory return a pointer that doesn't correspond to the requested byte range. If texture-backed memory is intended to be host-mappable, either honor offset/size (including mem->memory_offset) or reject non-zero offsets / non-whole-size mappings with VK_ERROR_MEMORY_MAP_FAILED to avoid undefined behavior.

The timeout logic mixes os_time_get_nano() (monotonic, unknown epoch) with timespec_get(TIME_UTC) + cnd_timedwait (wall-clock). This can make timeouts incorrect if the system clock changes and doesn't match the Vulkan runtime’s monotonic timeout semantics. Use the monotonic condvar helpers (u_cnd_monotonic_timedwait/u_cnd_monotonic_broadcast) with timespec_from_nsec(abs_timeout_ns), and handle thrd_timedout/error returns instead of ignoring rc.

VB cache defers set_vertex_buffers until DRAW, but the flush is guarded by vb_dirty which is only set on CmdBindVertexBuffers. Gallium requires set_vertex_buffers after each bind_vertex_elements_state before the next draw; Vulkan allows rebinding pipelines (vertex elements) without rebinding VBs. If vertex elements change without a subsequent CmdBindVertexBuffers, vb_dirty stays false here and set_vertex_buffers won’t be called, potentially violating the p_context.h contract and producing incorrect vertex fetch. Consider forcing a VB flush whenever the bound pipeline/vertex-elements state changes (e.g., mark vb_dirty on pipeline bind or track a separate flag).

nodes.body: In r300vk_get_format_properties(), the PIPE_BIND_DEPTH_STENCIL check unconditionally adds SAMPLED_IMAGE/TRANSFER/BLIT feature bits. PIPE_BIND_DEPTH_STENCIL only guarantees depth/stencil attachment usage; it does not imply the format is sampleable or blit-capable. This can cause vkGetPhysicalDeviceFormatProperties2 to over-report format capabilities. Consider only setting DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT here, and gate SAMPLED_IMAGE(_FILTER_LINEAR)/BLIT/TRANSFER bits based on the corresponding PIPE_BIND_SAMPLER_VIEW / PIPE_BIND_RENDER_TARGET support checks (or other verified conditions).

r300vk_get_format_properties() currently derives VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_2_UNIFORM_TEXEL_BUFFER_BIT from PIPE_BIND_CONSTANT_BUFFER on PIPE_BUFFER. Gallium constant buffers are untyped, so this doesn’t correspond to Vulkan uniform texel buffers and may incorrectly report support for many/most formats. Consider using PIPE_BIND_SAMPLER_VIEW with PIPE_BUFFER (and the appropriate pipe bindings for storage texel buffers if needed) when advertising texel-buffer format features.

r300vk_get_format_properties() sets linearTilingFeatures and optimalTilingFeatures to the same feature set. Gallium’s is_format_supported() doesn’t indicate VkImageTilingLinear support, so this can incorrectly advertise linear-tiling image support. If r300vk doesn’t implement VK_IMAGE_TILING_LINEAR images, linearTilingFeatures should be 0 (or otherwise computed independently) to avoid apps creating unsupported linear images.

When the hybrid-compute env gate is enabled, the physical device advertises VK_QUEUE_COMPUTE_BIT in queueFamilyProperties. However, r300vk_CreateComputePipelines() always returns VK_ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_PRESENT and the dispatch commands set a command-buffer error. Advertising a compute-capable queue while compute pipelines/dispatch are not supported is an API contract mismatch that can break apps/validation. Consider keeping VK_QUEUE_COMPUTE_BIT disabled until compute pipeline creation+dispatch are functional, or ensure the advertised compute queue is actually usable.

r300vk_CreateComputePipelines() returns VK_ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_PRESENT unconditionally. For createInfoCount==0, Vulkan patterns (and vk_common_CreateComputePipelines) return VK_SUCCESS after doing nothing; returning an error in the zero-count case can break callers that rely on that behavior. Consider special-casing createInfoCount==0 to return VK_SUCCESS.

Hybrid-compute enablement is read from getenv() in multiple places (limits init and queue-family query). This can lead to internally inconsistent properties if the environment changes between calls, and it also repeats getenv/strcmp on every query. Consider caching the decision in the physical-device object at creation/init time and using that stored value consistently for limits and queue flags.

On the no-submit path this calls `r300_trace_begin_trace` but never calls `r300_trace_finish_trace`. **<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Adjust synthetic stream for non-zero draw starts**

The synthetic stream is populated with `base + i` using `base = e->draw.first` / `e->draw.first_instance`, but the draw still submits `info.start = e->draw.first` and `info.start_instance = e->draw.first_instance`; Gallium then indexes vertex/instance attributes starting from those non-zero starts. With only `count` or `instances` elements allocated from index 0, any non-zero `firstVertex` or `firstInstance` makes fetches address beyond the synthetic buffer (and returns incorrect `gl_VertexIndex` / `gl_InstanceIndex`).

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Skip binding synthetic stream when buffer map fails**

If `pipe_buffer_map` fails (`map == NULL`), the function still binds `res` into `vb_cache` and schedules it for use, so the draw consumes uninitialized/stale buffer contents for synthetic system-value inputs. This creates undefined shader inputs under memory-pressure or mapping-failure conditions instead of a deterministic fallback/error path.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restrict system-value scan to reachable entrypoint code**

The new detector walks every function implementation in the shader, not just code reachable from the vertex entrypoint. If an unused helper function contains `gl_VertexIndex`/`gl_InstanceIndex`, it will still force `needs_*_stream` on, which can trigger unnecessary per-draw synthetic uploads or even pipeline creation failure on slot/binding limits despite the entrypoint never reading those system values.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Clamp synthetic stream size before allocating buffer**

The synthetic VB size is computed as `(uint64_t)count * sizeof(int32_t)` but stored in `pipe_resource.width0`, which is 32-bit; for very large draw counts this truncates the allocation size while the fill loop still writes `count` elements. That can write past the mapped allocation and corrupt memory instead of failing safely on oversized draws.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

The synthetic index stream buffer is sized for `count` elements, but vertex fetch uses the draw's `start` (and `start_instance` for instanced elements) when indexing attributes. For non-zero `firstVertex`/`firstInstance`, this will read past the end of the buffer. Also, `width0` is a 32-bit field: multiplying `count*sizeof(int32_t)` without overflow checks can truncate the allocation size and lead to OOB writes when filling the mapped buffer.

The synthetic vertex stream reserves slots based on `vertexAttributeDescriptionCount`, but shader input `driver_location` is derived from `var->data.location` (i.e., the shader’s `Location` decorations). If the shader uses non-zero-based or sparse locations (e.g., only location=1), `n_app` can collide with a real attribute slot and the appended velem will not match the shader’s expected input index.

These local `extern` declarations duplicate compiler-side APIs because r300vk can’t include r300_nir.h. This is brittle (signature drift won’t be caught) and makes it harder to track dependencies. Consider adding a small header that only declares the VS system-value helpers (without pulling in r300_screen.h), or refactoring r300_nir.h to avoid requiring r300_screen.h for these declarations.

Binding indices from Vulkan are 32-bit, but this code truncates them to `uint8_t` when computing the next free binding. If an app provides a binding >= 256 (or even just > R300VK_MAX_VERTEX_BINDINGS), truncation can pick a conflicting binding and the later limit check can be bypassed. This should validate bindings against R300VK_MAX_VERTEX_BINDINGS before casting/using them.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Gate synthetic VB rebinding on successful stream fill**

When synthetic stream allocation/mapping fails, `r300vk_bind_synthetic_index_stream` exits without updating `vb_cache`, but the draw path still marks the slot dirty and flushes vertex buffers. In that failure path, the synthetic binding is either left NULL (first use) or reuses a previous draw’s buffer contents, so shaders reading `gl_VertexIndex`/`gl_InstanceIndex` can consume stale/incorrect values under memory pressure. This should only mark/flush the synthetic binding when stream creation succeeds (or explicitly clear the slot and fail/skip the draw).

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Choose synthetic binding from attribute-used bindings only**

The synthetic stream binding is selected from the maximum of all `pVertexBindingDescriptions`, including bindings that are never referenced by any vertex attribute. If an unused binding occupies the top slot (e.g. binding 15), this logic forces `binding + synth > R300VK_MAX_VERTEX_BINDINGS` and pipeline creation fails with `VK_ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_PRESENT` even though lower free bindings exist and the shader would run. Restricting the scan to bindings actually used by `pVertexAttributeDescriptions` avoids these false negatives.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

nodes.body:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reapply dynamic viewport/scissor after tile selection**

Tiled replay now depends on `tile_origin_x/y`, but viewport/scissor state is only transformed at the original command position. Because `vkCmdSetViewport`/`vkCmdSetScissor` are valid both inside and outside a render pass, a command buffer that records them before `BEGIN_RENDER_PASS` will compute them with origin `(0,0)` and then reuse that stale state for tile passes `> 0`, so secondary tiles render/clamp in the wrong region. The replay path needs to re-derive or re-emit these states after tile origin is known for each pass.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep wide-lines feature disabled until it is implemented**

This change reports `wideLines` (and related optional raster features) as supported, but the graphics pipeline setup still hardcodes rasterizer state and does not consume application rasterization parameters such as requested line width. After this flag flip, applications and CTS are allowed to use `lineWidth != 1.0`, yet the driver path has no corresponding handling, so behavior will be incorrect while the feature is advertised as supported.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Ignore instance-rate bindings when clamping vertex draw count**

The new robust draw clamp treats every referenced vertex binding as per-vertex and uses `first_vertex`/`vertexCount` for all of them. For bindings declared with `VK_VERTEX_INPUT_RATE_INSTANCE`, this computes availability from the wrong index domain and can shrink draws to 0 or 1 vertices in valid instanced workloads, causing missing geometry whenever instance attributes are present.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Report sampleCounts from real format support, not a constant**

`vkGetPhysicalDeviceImageFormatProperties2` now unconditionally returns `VK_SAMPLE_COUNT_1_BIT | VK_SAMPLE_COUNT_4_BIT` for all image format/type queries, but `vkCreateImage` only learns actual support by attempting `resource_create`. For unsupported 4x combinations this advertises a capability the driver cannot satisfy, then creation falls through as allocation failure instead of format/parameter rejection, which breaks the query/create contract expected by applications.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve render-pass order when replaying tiled command buffers**

The new outer `tile_pass` loop replays the entire command stream once per tile, which interleaves distinct render passes as `RP0(tile0), RP1(tile0), RP0(tile1), RP1(tile1), ...` instead of completing earlier render-pass work before later pass commands. Any workload where a later pass consumes results from an earlier pass (with barriers/layout transitions between them) can observe partially rendered data, because only tile 0 of the producer pass has executed when the consumer pass runs.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**issue (bug_risk):** Freeing set descriptors with vk_free2 mismatches the vk_zalloc allocator used at allocation time.

Descriptors are allocated in r300vk_AllocateDescriptorSets() via vk_zalloc(&device->vk.alloc, ...), but here they are freed with vk_free2(&device->vk.alloc, pAllocator, ...). This mixes *2 and non-*2 allocator variants for the same memory, which breaks allocator pairing assumptions. Please either allocate with vk_zalloc2 (using pAllocator) or free with vk_free to match vk_zalloc.

**issue (bug_risk):** Descriptor set allocation is not atomic on failure, leaving the pool with partially allocated sets.

If the pool runs out of free slots (`!set`) or `vk_zalloc` fails, the function returns an error but leaves earlier sets from this call marked as allocated (`allocated` flag and `pool->allocated_sets`), and in the OOM path the output handles are not even nulled. Vulkan requires descriptor set allocation to be atomic per call. Please track which sets are newly allocated in this invocation and, on any failure, fully roll them back: free their descriptor arrays, finalize their `vk_object_base`, clear `allocated`, decrement `pool->allocated_sets`, and null the corresponding `pDescriptorSets` entries.

nodes.body: Silently truncating `descriptorSetCount` / `dynamicOffsetCount` will record a bind that is observably different from the API call (dropping sets/offsets), which can lead to incorrect resource bindings at replay time. Instead of clamping, treat this as a record-time error (fail the command buffer) or allocate variable-sized storage (e.g., from the cmd-buffer arena) so the full arrays are preserved; at minimum, avoid partially recording a bind.

Making `R300VK_CMD_BIND_DESCRIPTOR_SETS` a replay no-op means the replay path does not update any 'currently bound descriptor sets' state. Unless the `DISPATCH`/`DRAW` replay code scans the command stream to find the latest bind (which would be unusual and expensive), subsequent dispatch/draw replays will not know which sets/offsets to consume. Consider updating a replay context/state object here (store bound sets + dynamic offsets keyed by bind point / firstSet), and have dispatch/draw consume that state.

Clamping writes against `layout->total_descriptors` allows a write to spill into subsequent bindings even when they are a different descriptor type. The comment notes this is 'over-permissive', but it can still corrupt descriptor state for mixed-type layouts because it overwrites other bindings' slots. A safer approach is to clamp to the selected binding's remaining array size (`b->count - dstArrayElement`), and only implement cross-binding spill when adjacent bindings are consecutive and have identical descriptorType (per the spec rule referenced).

Like the write path, clamping copy spans against `total_descriptors` can copy across binding boundaries into unrelated bindings (possibly of different types), which can corrupt descriptor state for multi-binding layouts. Prefer clamping within the source/destination binding's remaining element counts, and only allow spill into adjacent bindings when they are consecutive and have the same descriptor type.

nodes.body: The comment for `use_txf` is misleading. The `use_txf` parameter of `util_make_fragment_tex_shader` selects between TXF (integer texel fetch) and TEX (filtered sample); it has no bearing on whether the sampler uses NEAREST vs LINEAR filtering — that is controlled by sampler state. The comment as written conflates these concepts and could mislead future maintainers. Consider rewording to e.g. "use_txf=false: use filtered TEX sample (filter mode set via sampler state)".

Silently demoting an identity-map pipeline to a no-op on shader synthesis failure may hide real issues (e.g. OOM from `util_make_*_shader`) and produce surprising runtime behavior where a dispatch becomes a no-op without any diagnostic. Consider at least logging a warning (e.g. via `mesa_logw` / `vk_debug_report`) so the silent fallback is observable. Additionally, a synthesis failure caused by allocation failure arguably warrants returning `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_HOST_MEMORY` rather than silently succeeding.

`device->pipe` (a `pipe_context`) is generally not thread-safe, but `vkCreateComputePipelines` can be called concurrently from multiple threads per the Vulkan spec. Calling `util_make_vertex_passthrough_shader` / `util_make_fragment_tex_shader` (which invoke `pipe->create_vs_state` / `create_fs_state`) on a shared context from concurrent pipeline creations is a race. Consider serializing access to `device->pipe` with a mutex, or using a per-thread/per-call context.

nodes.body: The lazy initialization in `r300vk_device_init_identity_map_state` reads and writes the four `identity_map_*_cso` fields on `device` without any locking. Vulkan permits concurrent `vkCreateComputePipelines`/`vkCreateGraphicsPipelines` calls on the same `VkDevice` from multiple threads, so two threads racing through the first identity-map pipeline creation can both observe a NULL pointer, both call `pipe->create_*_state`, and leak one CSO (and worse, since gallium `pipe_context` itself is generally not thread-safe, the concurrent `create_*_state` calls on the same `pipe` may corrupt internal context state). Consider guarding initialization with a mutex (e.g., a `simple_mtx_t` on the device) or performing eager initialization at device-create time when the pipe context is single-threadedly owned.

On a partial failure (e.g., blend succeeds, rasterizer creation later fails on a subsequent call), the successfully-created CSOs remain stored on the device and will be retried only for the NULL ones on the next call. That is fine for forward progress, but if `create_rasterizer_state` returns NULL here and the caller propagates the error, the partially-initialized state persists on the device until `DestroyDevice`. That is acceptable, but note that returning `false` from `r300vk_identity_map_synthesize_shaders` should be mapped to a proper `VkResult` (likely `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_HOST_MEMORY`) by the caller; please confirm the caller does so rather than silently failing pipeline creation.

Four parallel `void *` fields with the same lifecycle and the same `identity_map_` prefix would be more cohesive grouped into a small nested struct (e.g., `struct { void *blend, *rasterizer, *dsa, *sampler; } identity_map_cso;`). This also makes it easy to add a `bool initialized;` companion field if you later switch to eager init or a single-shot lazy guard. Optional.

If `r300vk_identity_map_dispatch_replay` can be called from multiple threads (Vulkan command buffer recording is commonly multi-threaded), two threads may race on the `getenv`/store. The race is benign in practice (both threads compute the same value), but a tool like TSan will flag it. Consider using a `static _Atomic int` (or `call_once`/pthread_once), or initializing the cache once at instance creation alongside the rest of the `R300VK_DEBUG` parsing already done in `r300vk_instance.c` so the gate stays consistent with other debug options.

Substring matching with `strstr` will produce false positives for any debug token that merely contains `identity_map` as a substring (e.g., `no_identity_map`, `identity_map_off`). For logging an opaque handle value, prefer printing it as `%" PRIx64 "` via a `(uint64_t)` cast so the diagnostic is correct on all targets.

nodes.body: Using `in_binding == out_binding` as the trigger for the layout-walk fallback is fragile and conflates two distinct cases. Per the companion change in `r300_compute_admission.c`, neither `input_ssbo_binding` nor `output_ssbo_binding` is set when the NIR sources aren't constants — both remain at their default (presumably 0), which happens to make them equal. However, if a future detector path or initialization sets these fields to non-zero but coincidentally equal values, the fallback will still trigger and silently override valid detector data; conversely, a kernel where the detector did capture distinct constant bindings that happen to be wrong won't get the fallback. Consider using an explicit sentinel (e.g., initializing both fields to `UINT32_MAX` in the detector and checking for that), or tracking a separate `bindings_resolved` boolean in `pl->identity_map`, so the fallback condition matches the actual semantic intent.

The 'Nth STORAGE_BUFFER in layout order == Nth SSBO referenced by the shader' assumption is a load-bearing invariant for correctness but is not enforced anywhere visible. Shaders are free to declare/use SSBOs in any binding order, and a kernel that reads from binding 1 and writes to binding 0 would have its input/output swapped by this fallback, silently producing incorrect results. Please either (a) document and assert this ordering contract at the kernel-authoring boundary, or (b) recover the actual binding indices from the NIR by tracing the `load_vulkan_descriptor` chain back to its `desc_set`/`binding` immediates rather than relying on declaration order.

These assignments only mutate `out->input_ssbo_binding` / `out->output_ssbo_binding` in the (per the new comment, never-occurring) constant case, leaving them at whatever value `out` carried on entry. The consumer in `r300vk_identity_map_dispatch_replay` then uses `in_binding == out_binding` to decide whether to fall back to the layout walk, which only works because both fields default to the same value (e.g., 0). Consider initializing these fields to an explicit sentinel here unconditionally (and removing the now-misleading constant-capture, since the diagnostic printf already logs the constness), so the contract with the consumer is explicit rather than relying on default-zero coincidence.

nodes.body: Folding `nir_op_imul` onto float `ureg_MUL` is not bit-exact even for UNORM8 round-trips: with byte operands `x,y` normalized to `x/255, y/255`, `MUL` yields `xy/65025`, which when re-encoded to UNORM8 gives `round(xy*255/65025) = round(xy/255)`, not the integer product `x*y` (or `x*y mod 256`) that NIR semantics require. The justification in the header comment about "FP24-budget envelope" applies to additive ops where the normalization factor cancels, not to multiplication. The same concern applies to `imin/imax/umin/umax` when the underlying NIR values are not in [0,1] UNORM form. Consider either removing the integer opcodes from the admitted set in `binary_map_op_admitted()` or restricting them to additive ops only.

The `else if` chain skips binary-map synthesis whenever `identity_map.is_identity_map` is true, even when identity-map synthesis succeeds (the common case). More importantly, if identity-map synthesis *fails* and clears the flag, this also skips binary-map synthesis — so a kernel that legitimately matched both detectors (or matched only binary-map but happened to have identity_map set true and fail) gets neither lowering. Consider replacing the `else if` with two independent `if` statements, or asserting/enforcing mutual exclusion between the two detection flags at detection time.

**issue:** Comment about preserving the previous slot value seems inconsistent with setting `slot->type = 0`

The behavior described in the comment doesn’t match the implementation: it says an out-of-bounds binding is “silently skipped (the previous slot's value ... persists)”, but the code sets `slot->type = 0` in that case. This comment violates the repository's source-comment hygiene rules (AGENTS.md:386-438): it embeds a dated, internal-repo path reference (`steinmarder src/re/r300/findings/active/2026-05-28-r300-pfs-no-flat-32bit-shader-address-falsified.md`) and a session date. Per AGENTS.md, source-code comments must avoid task/issue/PR refs, phase labels, session dates, and internal-repo paths; the rationale should be expressed in terms of durable mechanism names (e.g. "R300 PFS has no shader-emitted flat address, so out-of-bounds descriptor offsets cannot be clamped in NIR"). The cross-repo finding URL belongs in the commit message / steinmarder evidence tree, not in the driver source.

Silently dropping an out-of-bounds descriptor write by setting `slot->type = 0` and breaking has two concrete problems:

1. The comment claims "the previous slot's value, NULL after AllocateDescriptorSets's zalloc, persists." That is only true the first time a slot is written. `r300vk_UpdateDescriptorSets` can be called repeatedly to overwrite an existing binding, in which case `slot->buf.buffer` still holds the previously-bound `VkBuffer` handle (potentially for a buffer the app has since destroyed). Downstream consumers (`r300vk_identity_map_dispatch_replay` at `r300vk_identity_map.c:288-317`, binary-map at `:644-666`) test `slot->buf.buffer` for non-NULL and then `VK_FROM_HANDLE` it — they will dereference the stale handle. To make the "skip" safe, the buf union fields must be explicitly zeroed when rejecting.

2. Quietly rewriting the recorded `slot->type` to `0` (which is `VK_DESCRIPTOR_TYPE_SAMPLER`, not an "invalid" sentinel) on a malformed write hides an app bug that `VK_EXT_debug_utils` / validation layers normally flag, and aliases the slot as a sampler descriptor for any consumer that switches on `slot->type`. A more honest signal would be a `vk_errorf(... VK_ERROR_…)`-style log (consistent with other r300vk error sites) plus zeroing the whole slot, or — preferably — keeping the existing valid binding rather than partially clobbering it.

The premise of this change — that the captured `input_a_ssbo_binding` / `input_b_ssbo_binding` give the correct operand order for non-commutative ALU ops — is not actually guaranteed by the detector. In `r300_nir_detect_binary_map` (src/gallium/drivers/r300/r300_compute_admission.c:225-229), the matcher accepts both the `(s0==load_a, s1==load_b)` and `(s0==load_b, s1==load_a)` orderings, but then unconditionally records `input_a_ssbo_binding = load_a` and `input_b_ssbo_binding = load_b`, where `load_a` / `load_b` are simply the first and second `load_ssbo` instructions in NIR walk order (lines 196-200). For non-commutative ops admitted by `binary_map_op_admitted` (notably `nir_op_fsub` and `nir_op_isub`, src/gallium/drivers/r300/r300_compute_admission.c:159, 162), if NIR happens to emit the right-hand operand's load first, this orchestrator will pass it as `sv_a` (the "left" operand of the lowered ALU), producing the wrong result regardless of binding declaration order.

To deliver the property the comment claims, the detector needs to record which load corresponds to `alu.src[0]` vs `alu.src[1]` (e.g., swap `load_a`/`load_b` in the `ba` branch before capturing bindings), so that `input_a_ssbo_binding` truly identifies the left operand of the ALU op.

Additionally, the comment lists "SUB, DIV, MOD, SHL, SHR" as motivating non-commutative ops, but DIV/MOD/SHL/SHR are not in the admitted op set at all (src/gallium/drivers/r300/r300_compute_admission.c:158-167); only `isub` / `fsub` are non-commutative and admitted. The comment should be aligned with the actual admitted set to avoid misleading future readers.

The "all-zero ⇒ detector did not capture" heuristic conflates two distinct states: "detector saw no constant binding sources at all" and "detector captured a subset of bindings, one of which legitimately happens to be 0". Because `r300_nir_detect_binary_map` initializes all three fields to 0 and only overwrites those for which `nir_src_is_const` is true (src/gallium/drivers/r300/r300_compute_admission.c:174-177, 243-248), a partial-capture case (e.g., output is a const but input_a's source was lowered to a non-const handle) would leave `in_a_binding == 0` while `out_binding != 0`, making `detector_captured` true and silently routing operand A to whatever descriptor happens to live at binding 0 (typically a real but wrong buffer). Consider having the detector publish an explicit "captured" flag (e.g., a bitmask or bool) rather than overloading the all-zero sentinel, so the orchestrator can distinguish "fully captured" from "partially captured" from "not captured" and refuse the partial case.

nodes.body: The render target backing the 1×M bin row is never initialized/cleared before drawing points with additive blending. The blend-acc detector explicitly relies on the bin mask being “implicit in the buffer size” (i.e., gid & (M-1)), which only holds when M is a power of two. Consider rejecting non-power-of-two M (return false) or extending detection/replay to honor the actual mask.

The input buffer map reads N*sizeof(uint32_t) bytes starting at offset 0, but there’s no validation that the bound input buffer (or descriptor range) is large enough for N elements. Add a size/range check (and/or incorporate VkDescriptorBufferInfo offset/range) before mapping to avoid OOB CPU reads or driver assertions when dispatch dimensions exceed the input buffer length.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restrict ZPASS detection to replayed predicates**

For shaders whose `if` condition derives from the load but is not exactly `in_data[gid] != 0u` (for example `in_data[gid] == 0u` or `in_data[gid] >= threshold` as described in this comment), this detector still marks the pipeline as ZPASS-replayable, while the replay path hardcodes `pred = (in_words[gid] != 0u)`. That silently writes the count for a different predicate instead of falling back, so the detector needs to either prove/extract the exact predicate or reject shapes the orchestrator cannot reproduce.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Honor storage-buffer descriptor offsets**

When the app binds either storage buffer with a non-zero `VkDescriptorBufferInfo::offset`, descriptor updates preserve that offset/range in `r300vk_descriptor.c:357-359`, but this replay maps the underlying resource from byte 0 and later writes the result at byte 0 as well. Any ZPASS reduction using a suballocated predicate or counter buffer will read the wrong predicates and/or overwrite unrelated data instead of the descriptor range the shader addresses.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Tile ZPASS render targets beyond the R300 axis limit**

This path admits up to `2048 * 2048` invocations but then creates a single `width0 = N` render target. On the non-r500 R300/RS482 target, the screen advertises a 2048 2D texture axis limit (`r300_screen.c:551`), so dispatches with more than 2048 invocations can fail resource creation and fall through to the no-op compute lifecycle, leaving the counter unchanged; use the existing 2D tiling strategy or cap `N` to the actual width limit.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve atomicAdd's existing counter value**

For any dispatch where `count_out[0]` is already non-zero, or for multiple dispatches accumulating into the same counter, `atomicAdd(count_out, 1u)` must add the surviving-fragment count to the existing value. This replay overwrites the first word with only the query count, so it silently loses the prior counter contents instead of preserving the atomic-add side effect.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject non-zero atomic offsets for ZPASS replay**

At this point the detector has not checked `atomic->src[1]`, so it accepts conditional `atomicAdd` operations to any SSBO offset, such as `atomicAdd(counts[gid], 1u)` or `atomicAdd(count_out[1], 1u)`. The replay always writes a single total to `count_out[0]`, so these admitted shaders produce the wrong memory update unless the atomic offset is proven to be zero.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Account for compute local size in ZPASS replay**

For shaders declared with `local_size_x/y/z` greater than 1, Vulkan dispatch launches `group_count * local_size` invocations, but this replay sizes the draw and input scan using only the workgroup counts. Such shaders will count only the first workgroup-count predicates and draw too few fragments, so either multiply by the shader's local size or reject non-1 local sizes for this lowering.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Scalarize the KILL_IF predicate source**

For this synthesized FS, the vertex input provides only one predicate component, but `ureg_KILL_IF(ureg_src(tmp))` tests the whole vector; TGSI KILL_IF kills if any component is negative. Since the ADD writes `tmp.yzw` from undefined or default non-predicate channels minus 0.5, true predicates can still be discarded, making the ZPASS query return zero or otherwise undercount; use a scalar `.x` source for the kill test.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Verify the predicate load address matches gid**

The detector only proves that the `if` condition derives from the single load result, not that the load is `in_data[gid]`. A shader like `if (in_data[0] != 0) atomicAdd(count_out, 1u)` or `if (in_data[gid * 2] != 0) ...` is therefore admitted, but the replay scans `in_words[gid]`, so it counts a different predicate stream unless the load offset is matched to the supported gid mapping.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject 64-bit atomic counters**

If the shader uses a 64-bit `atomicAdd(..., 1ul)`, `nir_src_as_uint` still sees the constant value as 1 and this detector admits the kernel, but the replay always writes a saturated 32-bit value to the first four bytes of the counter. That produces the wrong result for valid 64-bit counter shapes, so the detector should require a 32-bit atomic value/counter or the replay must write the full 64-bit atomic result.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

`tgsi_ureg` doesn't provide a `ureg_KILL_IF` helper, and TGSI KILL_IF semantics kill the fragment if *any* component of the source is < 0 (not just `.x`). As written, `tmp.y/z/w` will be `in_pred.y/z/w - 0.5` (likely negative), so the shader will discard all fragments even when the predicate is 1.0, and it may also fail to compile due to the missing helper. Use a scalar-swizzled predicate and emit `TGSI_OPCODE_KILL_IF` via `ureg_insn`.

The ZPASS replay allocates a `1 x N` render target with `width0 = N`, but `N` is allowed up to `2048*2048` by the earlier bounds check. That width will exceed the R300 axis cap (2048) and cause `resource_create` to fail for most non-trivial dispatch sizes, effectively disabling the lowering. Consider mapping invocations onto a `width x height` grid using the existing `derive_raster_extent` helper (width <= 2048, height = ceil(N/width)) and computing per-gid point positions from `(gid % width, gid / width)`.

The VBO staging maps `N * sizeof(uint32_t)` bytes from the input buffer (`in_words[gid]` for gid in [0,N)). There is no check that `in_buf->size` is large enough, so a too-small descriptor can cause out-of-bounds reads during `buffer_map`/`memcpy`. Add an explicit size check before mapping.

The detector only checks that the atomic's block parent is a `nir_if`, but it doesn't verify the atomic is in the `then_list` (true branch). If the atomic is in the `else_list`, the detector would still match even though the semantics are inverted (it would count false predicates). Add an explicit check that `atomic_block->cf_node` is in `if_node->then_list`.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject multi-dimensional ZPASS dispatches**

When `group_count_y` or `group_count_z` is greater than 1, the documented supported shader shape still indexes `in_data[gl_GlobalInvocationID.x]`, so Vulkan repeats the same X predicate stream for each Y/Z lane. This replay instead computes `N = x * y * z` and later scans `in_words[0..N-1]` as if the shader used a flattened linear gid, so a dispatch like `(x=4, y=2, z=1)` counts predicates 0..7 instead of counting predicates 0..3 twice. Until the detector proves a flattened address, this path should reject non-1 Y/Z group counts or replay the X-indexed repetition.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject ZPASS atomics inside loops**

This only checks that the atomic block's immediate parent is an `if`, so a kernel such as `for (uint i = 0; i < 4; ++i) if (in_data[gid] != 0) atomicAdd(count_out, 1u);` still has one static `ssbo_atomic` and one load and is admitted. The replay draws one point per invocation and writes one count per true predicate, but the shader's atomic executes once per loop iteration, so loop-contained matches undercount unless the detector rejects any enclosing `nir_loop` or proves a single iteration.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Require both ZPASS bindings before skipping fallback**

If the detector recovers only one constant binding after explicit IO lowering, this `OR` treats the whole pair as captured and leaves the uncaptured side at the zero sentinel. For example, with an opaque predicate binding and a constant output binding 2, replay reads descriptor binding 0 instead of falling back to the first storage-buffer binding the shader actually uses, so partially-captured kernels can read or write the wrong SSBO; require both bindings to be captured or resolve the missing side positionally.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**issue (bug_risk):** Failure to map the final texture silently results in no output copy but still returns success.

When `rt_map` is NULL, the function skips the copy-back but still returns true, leaving stale data in the output buffer while signaling success. This should be treated as a failure (or at least logged as an error) so callers can detect it.

Likewise, if `out_bytes` is NULL, consider logging and/or failing instead of silently skipping the copy.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restrict multipass detection to the doubled-step kernel**

For loop kernels whose body contains `iadd`, `ishl`, `fadd`, or any multiply by a value other than exactly 2, this detector still marks the pipeline as `is_multipass_scan`, but the synthesized fragment shader later hard-codes every pass as `sample * 2.0`. That makes an admitted kernel such as `for (...) x += 1u; out[i] = x;` execute as repeated doubling instead of the SPIR-V semantics; until synthesis uses `step_op` and the operand value, this detector should only accept the exact doubling shape it can replay.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Return failure when a ping-pong sampler view is missing**

If `create_sampler_view` fails on any pass, this only breaks out of the loop and then copies the current texture back to the output buffer before returning `true`. Under resource pressure or a driver allocation failure, a `pass_count > k` dispatch can therefore report successful replay with only the first `k` doublings applied; this path should fail the replay instead of committing a partial result.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Honor descriptor offsets for the params buffer**

When the params storage-buffer descriptor is bound with a non-zero `VkDescriptorBufferInfo::offset`, this maps the underlying pipe resource from byte 0 and reads the wrong `pass_count`; the same replay then either performs the wrong number of ping-pong passes or rejects a valid dispatch. The descriptor update path stores `slot->buf.offset`, so this path should add that offset to the mapped box before reading the first uint32 of the descriptor range.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve uint carry and overflow when doubling**

For the exact advertised `uint x = x * 2u` kernel, this doubles four UNORM8 color channels independently, so values that need a byte carry or 32-bit wraparound are written incorrectly: for example input `0x00000080` with `pass_count = 1` should become `0x00000100`, but the low byte is multiplied and clamped in the red channel instead. Unless the admission path also proves every input byte stays in the no-carry envelope, the replay needs integer-compatible packing rather than per-channel UNORM multiplication.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Fail replay when output copyback mapping fails**

If the output buffer map fails during the final texture-to-buffer copyback, this silently skips the write and still returns `true`, leaving the caller with an apparently completed dispatch and stale output data. This can happen under allocation/map failures after all ping-pong passes have run, so the replay should propagate failure instead of treating an unwritten result as success.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

The detector treats the first recognized ALU anywhere in a loop as the scan step, without checking that it consumes the loop-carried value and feeds the `store_ssbo`; even loop-counter arithmetic can satisfy this. It also admits ops the synthesized FS does not implement. This can route unrelated looped kernels through a hard-coded doubling pass, so the match should trace the stored value back through the loop-carried step and only accept the exact operation/constant the lowering can reproduce.

If creating a sampler view fails, this only breaks out of the pass loop and then copies the last completed texture while returning success. That reports a completed dispatch with only a partial number of doublings; this path should unwind and return false (or otherwise signal failure) instead of producing a partial result.

The final copy treats a failed `texture_map` as a no-op and still returns true, leaving the destination SSBO unchanged while the queue believes the lowered dispatch succeeded. Please make this an error path that performs the existing cleanup and returns false so failed readback does not silently produce stale output.

A failed output-buffer map is also silently ignored, so the function can return success without writing the computed texture back to the storage buffer. This should follow an error/unwind path and return false rather than completing with stale output contents.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Constrain the detected doubling to the stored loop value**

For kernels that have one store, two SSBO loads, and any surviving `x + x`/`x * 2`/`x << 1` inside a loop, this marks the pipeline as `is_multipass_scan` without proving that the doubled SSA value is the loop-carried value eventually stored. For example, a loop can double an unrelated accumulator while the store writes `in[gid] + 1`; this detector still routes dispatch to the synthesized ping-pong shader, which writes repeated doublings of the first buffer instead of the SPIR-V store value. The detector needs to trace the store source back through the loop-carried phi/ALU chain before admitting the replay shape.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Avoid writing padded raster cells past the dispatch size**

For dispatches whose invocation count is above 2048 but not an exact multiple of 2048, `derive_raster_extent()` rounds the texture up to a full final row (for example 2049 becomes 2048x2), and this replay later copies `width * height` texels back to the output buffer. When the bound output range is large enough, those padded cells overwrite elements that no compute invocation should touch; when it is only sized for the dispatch, the final map can fail instead. The replay needs to mask or limit the last row to `total_invocations` elements rather than treating the padded rectangle as real work.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Multiply dispatch groups by the shader local size**

When the admitted compute shader declares a local size greater than 1, Vulkan runs `group_count * local_size` invocations, but this replay allocates and copies only the raw group-count product. A kernel such as `layout(local_size_x = 4)` dispatched with `groupCountX = 64` should update 256 elements, while this path processes only 64 and leaves the remaining outputs stale; the detector should either reject non-1 local sizes or store the NIR workgroup size and include it in `total_invocations`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Move Meson built-ins out of project options**

For `PROFILE=gororoba-terakan`, these four keys are Meson built-in options, but this machine file places them under `[project options]`; the Meson machine-file docs reserve that section for project-specific options and show built-ins under `[built-in options]`, and Mesa does not define project options named `optimization`, `debug`, `b_ndebug`, or `werror`. As a result the recommended `make configure PROFILE=gororoba-terakan HOSTENV=generic-x86-64-os` lane can fail at setup with unknown options instead of producing the intended `-Os` configuration; move these keys to a `[built-in options]` section like the existing x86-64-v1 profiles.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Disable draw LLVM in the Terakan lane**

On the Debian LLVM-21 hosts called out by the existing Terakan pump profile, this new profile leaves Mesa's `draw-use-llvm` default enabled while also enabling LLVM, which pulls in Gallium draw's LLVM JIT path and hits the documented `llvm::SectionMemoryManager` link failure even though r600+Terakan do not need that path. The sibling Terakan no-rusticl pump profile already sets `draw-use-llvm = false` for this exact lane, so the new recommended generic profile should carry the same option instead of reintroducing that host-specific link break.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Pin the generic lane to X11 platforms**

Because this profile never sets `platforms`, Mesa's Linux DRM default expands `auto` to both `x11` and `wayland` in `meson.build`, so the new recommended Terakan lane now requires/builds Wayland even though the lane only needs r600 GLX/DRM plus the Terakan Vulkan ICD. The existing Terakan pump profile documents the same Wayland path as a link hazard on the target Debian hosts (`wl_fixes_interface` from staging/fixes), so this portable generic profile should set `platforms = ['x11']` rather than relying on the auto default.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
